categories.name: Structure
categories.description: How data is organized — rows, columns, and the shape of your tables.

categories.name: Cleaning
categories.description: Finding and fixing errors, gaps, and inconsistencies in raw data.

categories.name: Transformation
categories.description: Reshaping, recoding, and deriving new values from what you have.

categories.name: Integration
categories.description: Combining data from multiple sources into one coherent view.

categories.name: Quality
categories.description: Rules, checks, and dimensions of trustworthy data.

concepts.title: Tidy Data
concepts.description: A dataset is tidy when every row is an observation and every column is a variable. This design pattern makes analysis straightforward in any tool.
concepts.details: Hadley Wickham's 2014 paper defines three rules: (1) each variable forms a column, (2) each observation forms a row, (3) each value is a single cell. Tidy data is not a file format — it is a design pattern that applies to CSV, SQL tables, JSON arrays, or Excel sheets.
concepts.examples: Survey: one row per respondent, columns for age, income, answers.  Gene expression: rows = genes, columns = samples.
concepts.pitfalls: Not all analysis needs tidy data. Some visualizations and models prefer wide format. Tidy ≠ simple.
concepts.related: Wide vs Long, One Observation Per Row, One Variable Per Column

concepts.title: Wide vs Long Format
concepts.description: The same data stored with repeated measures as columns (wide) or as rows (long). Neither is wrong — each serves different downstream purposes.
concepts.details: Wide: {ID, Score_T1, Score_T2, Score_T3}.  Long: {ID, Time, Value} stacked.  Converting wide→long is pivot_longer (melt); long→wide is pivot_wider (cast/dcast). Long is better for most statistical models and grouped plots; wide is often more readable for reporting.
concepts.examples: Employee performance: wide has Q1…Q4 as columns; long stacks quarters.  Patient vitals: wide has each timestamp as a column; long stacks them.
concepts.pitfalls: Widening can create hundreds of columns. Long format bloats row count. Column naming conventions differ.
concepts.related: Tidy Data, Pivoting, One Variable Per Column

concepts.title: One Observation Per Row
concepts.description: Each row should represent a single observational unit. Bundling multiple observations in one row breaks most analytical tools.
concepts.details: The unit of analysis defines what each row represents: a person, transaction, or timepoint. If a cell contains 'Alice, Bob, Carol' those need separate rows. Hierarchical data (children→families→neighborhoods) should be flattened into related tables.
concepts.examples: One row per survey respondent.  One row per purchase transaction.  One row per sensor reading.
concepts.pitfalls: Multiple observations in one cell cannot be filtered or joined. Aggregations produce wrong counts.
concepts.related: Tidy Data, Wide vs Long, Spreadsheet Problems

concepts.title: One Variable Per Column
concepts.description: Each column should contain values of a single variable type. Mixed variables in one column or one variable split across many columns violate this.
concepts.details: Common violations: a column 'Age_Group' containing '25-34' (two variables), column headers 'Jan_Sales, Feb_Sales' (time encoded in names). When variables are in column headers, reshape is needed.
concepts.examples: age, gender, location in separate columns.  height_cm, weight_kg in separate columns.
concepts.pitfalls: Combining variables loses type safety. Splitting variables creates column proliferation.
concepts.related: Tidy Data, Wide vs Long, Pivoting

concepts.title: Data Structure
concepts.description: The organization of data into tables, lists, hierarchies, or graphs determines what analyses are possible.
concepts.details: Tabular data (rows/columns) is most common but not only. Hierarchical (JSON trees) represent nested relationships. Graph structures (nodes/edges) represent networks. The structure choice drives all downstream operations.
concepts.examples: Relational tables: customers, orders, products.  JSON: nested addresses.  Graph: social networks.
concepts.pitfalls: Wrong structure forces costly transforms later. Flat↔hierarchical conversion introduces complexity.

concepts.title: Missing Values
concepts.description: Missing data occurs when no value is stored for a variable. Handling it is one of the most critical steps in cleaning.
concepts.details: Three mechanisms (MCAR/MAR/MNAR): MCAR — random, unrelated to any values. MAR — depends on observed data. MNAR — depends on the missing value itself (hardest). Strategies: deletion, imputation (mean/mode, model-based, multiple), leaving blank.
concepts.examples: Survey skips (MAR).  Sensor failures (MCAR).  Income non-response by high earners (MNAR).
concepts.pitfalls: Deletion introduces bias if not MCAR. Simple imputation underestimates variance.

concepts.title: Outliers
concepts.description: Observations that deviate substantially from others. May be genuine extremes or data entry errors.
concepts.details: Detection: z-score (±3 σ), IQR (Q1−1.5·IQR, Q3+1.5·IQR), box plots, scatter plots. Key question: real or erroneous? Real outliers carry information; erroneous ones should be fixed or removed.
concepts.examples: Height 270 cm (error) vs 210 cm (extreme but real).  Test score −5 (error) vs 99/100 (extreme).
concepts.pitfalls: Automatic removal loses real extremes. Keeping all distorts means and variance.

concepts.title: Duplicate Records
concepts.description: Same observation appearing more than once. Arises from entry errors, system bugs, or logging quirks.
concepts.details: Exact (all columns identical) vs partial (matching key fields only). Resolution: keep one, merge, or flag. Prevention: unique constraints.
concepts.examples: Customer database with same person entered twice.  Sensor logging same reading twice.
concepts.pitfalls: Removing all duplicates may erase legitimate repeats. Keeping all inflates counts.

concepts.title: Type Conversion
concepts.description: Changing data from one type to another (text→number, text→date, number→text) to make it usable.
concepts.details: Each conversion carries risk: parse failures, precision loss, silent concatenation ('12'+'34'='1234'). Best practice: inspect before batch converting, handle failures explicitly.
concepts.examples: Currency '$1,234' → 1234.  Date 'Jan 15 2024' → 2024-01-15.  Boolean 'yes/no' → true/false.
concepts.pitfalls: Implicit conversions cause silent errors. Date format ambiguity (MM/DD vs DD/MM).

concepts.title: Standardization
concepts.description: Making data consistent in naming, format, and units across a dataset or sources.
concepts.details: Naming (age vs Age), units (meters vs feet), coding (M/F vs Male/Female), dates (ISO 8601), encoding (UTF-8). Goal: a canonical form for all values.
concepts.examples: Country names → ISO alpha-2 codes.  Phone numbers → E.164 format.  Temperatures → Celsius.
concepts.pitfalls: Over-standardization loses nuance. Standards may conflict across sources.

concepts.title: Normalization
concepts.description: Adjusting values to a common scale without distorting differences.
concepts.details: Min-max: scales to [0,1] via (x−min)/(max−min).  Z-score: centers at mean, unit variance via (x−μ)/σ.  Decimal scaling. Critical for distance-based algorithms where large-scale variables dominate.
concepts.examples: Salary (0–200000) + Age (0–100) → both on [0,1] or μ=0,σ=1.  Exam scores from different ranges → comparable.
concepts.pitfalls: Min-max is outlier-sensitive. Z-score assumes near-normal. Neither preserves original distribution.

concepts.title: Binning / Discretization
concepts.description: Converting continuous values into discrete categories (bins/buckets).
concepts.details: Equal-width (N equal intervals) vs equal-frequency (same count per bin). Reduces noise, simplifies modeling, aids interpretability.
concepts.examples: Age continuous → bins [0-17, 18-34, 35-54, 55+].  Income → Low/Med/High.  Score → A/B/C/D/F.
concepts.pitfalls: Too few bins lose info; too many add noise. Continuous→categorical loses information.

concepts.title: Recoding Variables
concepts.description: Changing variable values to a new set — simplify, standardize, or re-categorize.
concepts.details: Value replacement (yes→1).  Range recoding (age 0-17 → 'minor').  Reverse coding (Likert scale directions). Preserves variable identity.
concepts.examples: Likert 1-5 → 5-1 for reversed items.  Binary: age≥18 → 1, else → 0.
concepts.pitfalls: Over-recoding loses distinctions. Downstream users may not realize recoding occurred.

concepts.title: Deriving Variables
concepts.description: Creating new variables from existing ones via math, logic, or text operations.
concepts.details: Arithmetic: BMI = kg/m².  Logical: is_minor = (age < 18).  Aggregation: total = sum across columns.  String: extract_area_code. Always create in new columns.
concepts.examples: BMI from weight/height.  Purchase frequency = purchases/months_active.
concepts.pitfalls: Too many derived variables create maintenance burden. Circular dependencies create logical issues.

concepts.title: Pivoting
concepts.description: Reshaping data by converting row values to columns (wide) or columns to rows (long).
concepts.details: Pivot_wider: unique values from one column → columns, values placed in cells.  Pivot_longer: multiple columns stacked into one column. Changes structure, not content.
concepts.examples: Monthly sales by product: long→wide.  Survey Q1-Q10 wide→long.
concepts.pitfalls: Can create hundreds of columns. Column naming gets complex. Not always reversible.

concepts.title: Reshaping Data
concepts.description: Changing the structure of a dataset while preserving its informational content.
concepts.details: Stack/concatenate rows.  Transpose (swap rows/columns).  Unnest (expand arrays). Raw data rarely arrives in optimal shape.
concepts.examples: Appending monthly CSVs.  Stacking quarterly results.  Expanding list-columns into rows.
concepts.pitfalls: Wrong keys produce silently wrong results. Row duplication in cross joins.

concepts.title: Joining Data
concepts.description: Combining two tables by matching values in common columns. Join type determines which rows appear.
concepts.details: Five types: Inner (both match).  Left (all left + matching right, null where none).  Right (all right).  Full (both, null where none).  Cross (Cartesian product).
concepts.examples: Customers LEFT JOIN Orders (keep all customers).  Products INNER JOIN Categories (categorized only).
concepts.pitfalls: Duplicate keys cause row multiplication. Null keys cause unexpected behavior. Column name conflicts need renaming.

concepts.title: Merging Data
concepts.description: Combining datasets by a common key. Merge and join are often used interchangeably.
concepts.details: Keys: primary (unique per row), foreign (references another table), composite (multiple columns). Match: exact, fuzzy, or range-based.
concepts.examples: Employee + Department on dept_id.  Sales + Product on product_code.
concepts.pitfalls: Key mismatches ('CA' vs 'California'). Memory issues at scale. Duplicates cause multiplication.

concepts.title: Concatenation
concepts.description: Stacking rows from tables with compatible structures. No matching needed.
concepts.details: Requirements: same column names (or mapped), compatible types, same conceptual structure. Common: combining time periods, regions, survey waves.
concepts.examples: Monthly CSVs → yearly file.  Multiple survey waves.  Regional data appended.
concepts.pitfalls: Column mismatches need pre-alignment. New columns create nulls in others.

concepts.title: Data Integration
concepts.description: Combining data from different sources into a unified view. Goes beyond simple joins.
concepts.details: Schema matching, entity resolution, conflict resolution, temporal alignment, key generation. Integration is the highest level of data merging.
concepts.examples: CRM + analytics + support tickets.  ERP + banking.  Multi-study meta-analysis.
concepts.pitfalls: Schema mismatches require manual mapping. Entity resolution errors corrupt results.

concepts.title: Aggregation
concepts.description: Summarizing multiple observations into a single value. The process of going from detail to summary.
concepts.details: Functions: count, sum, mean, median, min, max, std dev. Always 'by' something (group by). Each unique key combination produces one summary row.
concepts.examples: Average income by country.  Total sales by month.  Count customers by region.
concepts.pitfalls: Aggregation loses individual detail — cannot recover raw data from summaries.

concepts.title: Rollup / Grouping
concepts.description: Creating hierarchical summaries by aggregating at multiple levels simultaneously.
concepts.details: Rollup computes subtotals and grand total. Group by with cube/rollup produces summaries at every hierarchy level (Region→Country→Year).
concepts.examples: Sales: rollup by Region→Country→Product.  Employee: Department→Team→Individual.
concepts.pitfalls: Grows exponentially with dimensions. Users may misinterpret subtotals.

concepts.title: Sampling
concepts.description: Selecting a subset of observations to represent a larger set.
concepts.details: Simple random, stratified, systematic, cluster, weighted. Trade-off: larger samples more representative but more expensive.
concepts.examples: 1000 respondents from 10M population.  A/B test random sample.  1% sample for prototyping.
concepts.pitfalls: Sampling error is inherent. Biased sampling misleads. Small samples miss rare patterns.

concepts.title: Data Quality Dimensions
concepts.description: Quality is multidimensional. Six core dimensions: accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness.
concepts.details: DQIF framework. Each dimension is independent — a dataset can be accurate but incomplete, valid but not timely.
concepts.examples: Patient records: accurate diagnoses but incomplete follow-up.  Sales: complete but inconsistent across regions.
concepts.pitfalls: Focusing only on accuracy misses completeness issues. Quality is context-dependent.

concepts.title: Validation Rules
concepts.description: Explicit conditions data must satisfy: range, pattern, cross-field, referential, and business rules.
concepts.details: Range: age 0-150.  Pattern: email regex.  Cross-field: end_date > start_date.  Referential: valid country code exists.  Business: product must have price.
concepts.examples: Email must match pattern.  Postal code must be 5 digits.  Invoice = price × quantity.
concepts.pitfalls: Too many rules make entry difficult. Cross-field rules are expensive to check at scale.

concepts.title: Entity Resolution
concepts.description: Determining whether two records refer to the same real-world entity (record linkage, deduplication).
concepts.details: Exact matching, deterministic (rules-based), probabilistic (weighted similarity), ML-based. One of the hardest problems — no perfect solution.
concepts.examples: Customer DB: 'John Smith, 123 Main' vs 'J. Smith, 123 Main St'.  Hospital records merge.
concepts.pitfalls: False positives and false negatives have different costs. Open-world matching is impossible perfectly.

concepts.title: Imputation
concepts.description: Filling missing values with estimated values instead of deleting or leaving blank.
concepts.details: Simple: mean/median/mode.  KNN: impute from K most similar.  Regression: predict from other variables.  Multiple imputation: create M datasets, pool (gold standard). Method depends on missingness mechanism.
concepts.examples: Median income for non-respondents.  KNN for gene expression.  MICE for complex survey missingness.
concepts.pitfalls: Simple imputation underestimates variance. Wrong model → wrong imputation. MNAR data cannot be imputed properly without modeling missingness.

concepts.title: Grammar of Data
concepts.description: A unified theory: all data manipulation is a composition of four operations — selection, mutation, summarization, joining.
concepts.details: Wickham (2014): selection (rows/columns), mutation (add/change columns), summarization (reduce rows), joining (combine tables). SQL SELECT is selection+mutation; GROUP BY is summarization; JOIN is joining.
concepts.examples: SQL: SELECT, GROUP BY, JOIN.  pandas: groupby().agg(), merge().  dplyr: filter, mutate, summarise, join.
concepts.pitfalls: The grammar is abstract — doesn't tell you WHEN to use which. Complex pipelines are hard to debug.

concepts.title: Data Pipelines
concepts.description: Automated sequence of steps that transform raw data from raw data into analysis-ready form.
concepts.details: Components: source → ingestion → transformation → validation → sink. Good pipelines are idempotent, observable, versioned, tested.
concepts.examples: Daily ETL to data warehouse.  Real-time sensor stream processing.  ML preprocessing pipeline.
concepts.pitfalls: Complexity grows with sources. Debugging long chains is difficult. Schema changes break steps.

concepts.title: Spreadsheet Problems
concepts.description: Spreadsheets are ubiquitous but problematic: no schema enforcement, structural flexibility, no version control, hidden metadata, limited scale.
concepts.details: (1) No enforced schema — any cell any type. (2) Merged cells, multiple tables per sheet. (3) No version control. (4) Formulas invisible to tools. (5) ~1M row limit. (6) Email attachments → version drift.
concepts.examples: Dates stored as text in some cells, numbers in others.  Merged cells hiding data.  Multiple tables on one sheet.
concepts.pitfalls: Spreadsheet mindset treats data as flexible canvas — this is both strength and weakness.
concepts.related: Missing Values, Type Conversion, Structure, Quality
